comment: Authoritative sources only. The organising principle: never monitor an individual municipality's own website. Monitor the state-level register that the municipality is legally required to report into. Ohio's ~600 municipalities collapse to one Department of Taxation file; Pennsylvania's ~2,500 Act 32 jurisdictions collapse to one DCED register. That is what turns '7,400 jurisdictions' into roughly 60 things to watch.

sources.title: US DOL — FUTA Credit Reduction States
sources.expectedChange: annual, finalised each November

sources.title: US DOL — Significant Measures of State UI Tax Systems (every state's taxable wage base)
sources.expectedChange: annual, published with a lag
sources.note: THE BACKSTOP for every state's UI taxable wage base in one document. Registered after a direct question exposed a real gap: 40 of 51 state sources point at a REVENUE department's withholding guide, which covers income tax and says nothing about unemployment insurance — Alabama's booklet states outright that 'State unemployment tax... [is] not administered by the Department of Revenue'. So a state moving its wage base or new-employer rate would not have changed any document being watched. This one covers all 51. Verified to contain e.g. 'TEXAS ... Fixed 9,000 ... Taxable Wage Base ($)'. KNOWN LIMIT: it LAGS — DOL publishes annually and the 2024 edition is still newest as of 2026-08 (the 25 and 26 filenames both 404), so it confirms a change late rather than promptly. That is why per-state labor-department sources are registered alongside it: those are timely, this is the one that is always there. Covers the WAGE BASE reliably; per-employer experience rates are not a jurisdiction constant and are never monitorable.

This is Akamai/Cloudflare-style refusal of a cloud/datacenter IP range, which no header change fixes. One of the highest-value sources in the registry (the OASDI wage base), so excluded from the staleness test rather than pinning overall health red forever, but check it by hand each October when the COLA lands.

sources.title: Kentucky Secretary of State — Occupational License Tax Database (KRS 67.766), all districts
sources.expectedChange: rolling; most effective dates are 1 January, but a district can change its ordinance any time
sources.note: ADDED 2026-09-01, closing a real gap: this project's own data file already called this database 'Kentucky's PA-DCED/OH-Finder equivalent — an authoritative, state-run roster of 230 taxing districts', but nothing watched it, because it isn't a URL a plain GET can read: it's an ASP.NET WebForms page where the 227 district names load in a <select> but each district's actual rate only appears after a postback selecting it, into a panel that starts empty. harvester/ky-occupational-fetch.ts drives that postback for every district in one session (one GET for the viewstate/cookie, confirmed reusable across all 227 POSTs — verified by hand against three different districts before building this) and concatenates each district's name/ordinance/basis/rate/min/cap into one document, sorted by district id so only real content changes move the hash. Deliberately excludes each district's listed contact name/email/phone/address — administrative metadata and, for a real person's contact details, not something this project should be hashing and git-committing for no reason. Marked heavyFetch (227 requests, not 1) so the daily sweep's normal 'check everything, every day' does not force this specific source daily — see RegisteredSource.heavyFetch in run.ts — but the annual-new-year calendar window still forces it regardless, which is exactly when KY local rates actually move. A single unreadable district fails the WHOLE fetch rather than silently publishing a partial roster, matching this project's standing rule that a failed read is not the same as 'unchanged'.

sources.title: Ohio The Finder — JEDD/JEDZ tax rates (CSV)
sources.expectedChange: rolling; JEDDs are created by contract between a township and a municipality
sources.note: A direct CSV API rather than a download page — columns are EffStartDate,EffEndDate,JEDD_ID,Name,Rate, so a future parser can diff rate-by-rate instead of document-by-document. FIXED 2026-09-01: the direct api.thefinder.tax.ohio.gov URL 401s with {"errorCode":"BFF4002"} for any client — it is a backend-for-frontend API the public site's own browser bundle never calls directly either. Found by downloading and reading thefinder.tax.ohio.gov's own Next.js JS chunks: the site's file-download buttons all route through a SAME-ORIGIN proxy route, `/api/file-downloads/content?target=<url-encoded real API URL>`, which is what this URL now points at. Verified: 200, real CSV body, byte-identical across two fetches two seconds apart, so it hashes stably. If this ever 401s again, re-derive the proxy path from the current JS bundle rather than guessing headers — that is what fixed it this time after header/cookie/Referer guessing all failed.

sources.title: Ohio Dept of Taxation — Municipal Income Tax Rate Database (The Finder)

sources.title: Texas — UI taxable wage base (via US DOL Significant Measures of State UI Tax Systems)
sources.expectedChange: annual; unemployment wage base and employer rate schedule are set each autumn
sources.note: REPOINTED after twc.texas.gov proved unfetchable by any machine: every path tried returns an HTTP 202 WAF challenge instead of the page — the rates page, the no-www variant, an alternate rates path, the news index, and even a PDF under /sites/default/files. The block is domain-wide, not path-specific. Three other routes were tried and rejected: statutes.capitol.texas.gov is an Angular SPA that serves only a shell to a plain fetch (same failure class as the Municode wall already documented for Birmingham); law.justia.com 403s; data.texas.gov fetches but carries no wage-base figure. This DOL report is the one authoritative, fetchable source that does: verified it contains the row 'TEXAS ... Fixed 9,000 ... Taxable Wage Base ($)', independently corroborating the 9000 in data/states/TX-2026.json. TWO HONEST LIMITS. (1) It LAGS: DOL publishes annually and the 2024 edition is still the newest as of 2026-08 (the 25 and 26 filenames both 404), so a wage-base change would surface here late rather than promptly — a late signal being strictly better than the none we had. (2) It covers the UI wage base only, not income-tax withholding — which costs nothing HERE, because Texas levies no income tax and the wage base is the only figure in its data file that can move, and DOL's own report calls it 'Fixed'. Do NOT copy this URL to a state that has an income tax; for those, the state's own withholding guide remains the source. The same report does cross-check every state's wage base, so it is worth reading directly when auditing suiEmployer figures.

uiCoverage.$comment: How well each state's UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE figures (suiEmployer.wageBase, newEmployerRate, experienceRange) are actually watched — tracked separately because it is a different question from income-tax withholding, answered by a different agency, in a different document. This block exists because a direct question exposed that 40 of 51 states were pointed only at a REVENUE department's withholding guide, which carries no UI figures at all; Alabama's booklet says so in as many words.
uiCoverage.backstopOnlyMeaning: These states have NO dedicated labour-department source registered, so their UI figures are covered only by dol-ui-wage-bases. That backstop is real but LAGS (DOL publishes annually; the 2024 edition is still newest as of 2026-08) and carries the taxable WAGE BASE only — not new-employer rates or rate schedules. Treat a UI change in these states as something that will be confirmed late, not caught promptly.
uiCoverage.whyNotAllFifty: Four passes of path-probing plus per-state searching took this from 10 states to 47. The last four resisted. ARKANSAS and ARIZONA refuse automated clients outright — HTTP 403 to every path and header combination tried, the same class of block as Texas's WAF, and no amount of URL-hunting fixes a refusal to serve. NEBRASKA and OKLAHOMA have live agency domains but roughly ten candidate paths each were tried across three passes and none carried rate or wage-base figures; both appear to put rates behind an employer login (neworks.nebraska.gov, eztaxexpress.oesc.state.ok.us), which is not fetchable and arguably not public. Nothing was registered for these four rather than registering a page that would look monitored without being monitored — the DC and Ohio department homepages were rejected on exactly that principle earlier, and both states were later found properly at dedicated tax pages. Their wage base is still covered by the lagging DOL report; their new-employer rates are not covered at all.
uiCoverage.neverMonitorable: An individual employer's EXPERIENCE-RATED contribution rate is not a jurisdiction constant — it depends on that employer's own layoff history and is assigned to them privately. No source can carry it, which is why the engine takes it from input.employer.stateUnemploymentRate and falls back to the published new-employer rate. Only the wage base and the published schedules are monitorable at all.
uiCoverage.howCoverageIsCounted: From an explicit coversUI flag on each source, not inferred from the URL. The regex that preceded it mis-classified Florida — its reemployment-tax rate page IS Florida's UI source, but the domain contains no labour-ish word — which is the sort of quiet miscount that makes a coverage number worth less than the confidence it creates.

contentAudit.method: Each UI source's most recent capture searched for a taxable-wage-base phrase beside a dollar figure, and for percentage rate figures. Run against snapshots on disk.
contentAudit.whatThisChanged: The registration check accepted any page carrying a wage base OR rates, but every title claimed both. This audit separates them, and the result is materially weaker than the earlier headline: of 47 UI sources, only 29 states have a source that actually states a taxable WAGE BASE and 37 one that states RATES. Thirteen carry rates alone — verified as a property of the page, not a formatting mismatch: North Dakota, New York, Massachusetts, New Mexico, Iowa, South Carolina, Minnesota and Kansas contain no wage-base phrase anywhere. Four (Maryland, Minnesota, New Mexico, West Virginia) carry NEITHER and are now flagged monitoringGap, because a source that fetches cleanly while containing nothing is the failure this project already hit once with Pennsylvania's search form. Titles have been corrected to say what each source actually carries.
contentAudit.staleAfterUrlChanges: STALE as of the MI/NJ/VA/WY/NM url changes in this commit: these counts and the per-source uiContent classifications were computed against the PREVIOUS urls. The changed sources have had their uiContent removed rather than left asserting something about a page they no longer point at — missing is honest, stale is not. Run `npm run harvest:daily` then `npm run harvest:audit` to recompute; the new urls were each verified by direct probe (MI, NJ, VA, WY carry both figures; NM's new page carries rates) but that verification is not the same as a recorded audit against a stored capture.
